title: Semiconservative Replication Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll unzip a DNA helix and copy it the semiconservative way.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology — semiconservative DNA replication, helicase, DNA polymerase, leading and lagging strands, Okazaki fragments and ligase.
final_note: You learned that DNA is copied semiconservatively, helicase unwinds, DNA polymerase adds 5' to 3', the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase.

walkthroughs.body_html:
DNA replicates so each daughter molecule has one original strand and one new strand.

This was confirmed in 1958 by Meselson and Stahl: E. coli grown on heavy ¹⁵N then transferred to ¹⁴N → after one round, all DNA was intermediate density.

Conservative (both strands old in one, both new in the other) and dispersive (mixed throughout) models were ruled out.

At a replication origin, helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases → forms a replication fork.

DNA polymerase reads the template 3' → 5' and builds the new strand 5' → 3', using free nucleotides paired by complementary bases (A-T, C-G).

The two new bonds formed are phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Because polymerase only works 5' → 3', the two strands behave differently.

- Leading strand: synthesised continuously, following the unwinding fork.
- Lagging strand: synthesised in short Okazaki fragments away from the fork.

DNA ligase seals the gaps between fragments, joining the sugar-phosphate backbone.

Result: two identical DNA molecules, each one old + one new strand.
